cues.x: The Body Keeps the Score, by Bessel van der Kolk.

I want to begin on the fifth of July, 1978, in a Veterans Administration clinic in Boston, with a young Dutch psychiatrist who has just started his first proper job and a man sitting across from him who has not slept properly in ten years.
The psychiatrist is Bessel van der Kolk.
The patient's name, in the book, is Tom.
He is a lawyer, married, with children, successful by every outward measure.
He has come in the day after Independence Day, and the reason is the fireworks.
The night before, the noise had driven him into his car, where he sat for hours in a parking lot drinking, because being around his own family with that sound in the air was unbearable.
Tom had been a Marine in Vietnam.

He tells van der Kolk, in fragments, about a patrol in which his platoon was ambushed, about a close friend who was killed, and about what the platoon did afterwards, which was to enter a village and kill people who were not soldiers, including children.

He tells him that he has nightmares nearly every night, that he has held the same job and the same marriage for a decade while being emotionally absent from both, that he cannot bear to be close to his wife or his children, and that he sometimes feels more comfortable and more alive in the memory of the war than he does at his own dinner table.
And then van der Kolk offers him medication, and Tom refuses.
He says something that reorganises the young psychiatrist's entire career.
He says that if he takes the drugs and stops the nightmares, he will have abandoned his friends.
That their deaths will become meaningless.
That the nightmares are a kind of loyalty, and a memorial, and that giving them up would be a desertion.
Van der Kolk went to the hospital library afterwards to read up on what he was dealing with.
He found essentially nothing.
The books on what earlier generations had called shell shock and war neurosis had been removed from the shelves after the Second World War, on the assumption that the subject was closed.
There was, in 1978, no diagnosis of post traumatic stress disorder.
It did not exist as an official category and would not until 1980.
So he spent the next forty years working it out, and this book is the result.
It has sold in enormous numbers, spent years on bestseller lists, and become the book people give to each other when something has happened to them that they cannot explain to anybody.
The sentence at the centre of it is this: trauma is not the story of something that happened long ago.
It is the imprint left by that experience on the mind, the brain, and the body.
And crucially, that imprint is not a memory in the ordinary sense.

It is a set of physical, automatic responses that continue to fire in the present, in circumstances that have nothing to do with the original event, in a body that has not received the news that the danger is over.
Let me take you through the argument properly, because it builds in stages and the practical part at the end only makes sense if you have the mechanism.
But first, a word about how the diagnosis came to exist at all, because the history explains a great deal about why so many people go undiagnosed even now.
Van der Kolk points out that this discovery has been made and forgotten repeatedly for well over a century.
Charcot and Janet in Paris in the 1880s studied it in traumatised women.

British doctors documented it in soldiers in the First World War and called it shell shock, and the British authorities were sufficiently uncomfortable with the implications that official use of the term was discouraged.

American psychiatrists documented it again after the Second World War, in a study of men who had broken down in combat, and then the profession largely dropped the subject and the books were taken off the library shelves.
Each time, the finding was the same, and each time it was allowed to lapse.

Van der Kolk's explanation for that pattern is uncomfortable and, I think, correct: acknowledging what trauma does obliges you to acknowledge what caused it, and the causes are usually war, or the family, or institutions, none of which anybody in authority is keen to examine.
What broke the cycle in the 1970s was not a scientific breakthrough.
It was political organisation by Vietnam veterans, working with a small number of psychiatrists who took them seriously, who pushed until a diagnosis was formally created.
Post traumatic stress disorder entered the American diagnostic manual in 1980, two years after Tom sat in that office.
For the first time there was a name, which meant there could be research funding, treatment programmes, and a language a person could use to describe what was happening to them.
And van der Kolk notes the deep irony of what happened next.
The diagnosis was built almost entirely around adults who had experienced discrete, identifiable, catastrophic events: combat, assault, disasters.
Which meant it fitted Tom rather well, and fitted almost nobody in his subsequent caseload, because the majority of people he went on to treat had not survived one terrible day.
They had survived a childhood.
Start with what the brain is actually doing.
Van der Kolk gives a model that is simple enough to hold in your head and accurate enough to be useful.
Think of the brain as built in layers, from the bottom up, in the order they develop.
At the bottom is the reptilian brain, the brainstem, which runs breathing, heart rate, sleep, hunger, and the basic alarm systems.
It is fully operational at birth and it does not think, it only reacts.
Above that is the limbic system, the emotional brain, which develops in the first years of life and is shaped enormously by experience.
Its job is to decide, continuously and without consulting you, whether things are safe or dangerous.

And on top of that is the neocortex, and particularly the prefrontal cortex behind your forehead, which handles language, planning, reflection, and the ability to imagine a future different from the present.
Inside that system, two structures matter most for this book, and van der Kolk gives them names that stick.
The amygdala is the smoke detector.
Its job is to scan incoming information for threat and, if it finds any, to trigger the stress response instantly, before you are conscious of anything at all.
It is fast, and it is deliberately crude, because in evolutionary terms the cost of a false alarm is trivial and the cost of a missed alarm is death.
The medial prefrontal cortex is the watchtower.
It sits above the situation, takes in the wider picture, and can say: yes, that was a loud noise, but it is a car backfiring, and we are in a supermarket car park, and nothing is wrong.
It calms the smoke detector down.
Normal functioning is a working relationship between the two.
Trauma, van der Kolk argues, is a durable change in that relationship: a smoke detector set far too sensitive, and a watchtower that goes offline exactly when you need it.
And he has pictures.
In the 1990s, brain imaging became available, and van der Kolk and colleagues ran a study that is one of the most quoted findings in the field.
They took people with post traumatic stress, put them in a scanner, and played them a recorded script describing their own traumatic experience in detail, in the present tense, in their own words.
Then they watched what the brain did.
Three things happened.
First, activity increased sharply in the limbic areas on the right side of the brain, the emotional, non verbal, alarm side, and in the visual cortex.
The person was not remembering.
They were seeing it.
The brain was responding as though the event were happening now.
Second, the prefrontal watchtower went quiet.
The part of you that can say "this is a memory, I am safe, it is 2004 and I am in a laboratory in Boston" was, at that moment, largely switched off.
And third, the finding that gave the field one of its defining images: activity dropped in Broca's area, which is the speech production centre of the brain.
It is the region that, when damaged by a stroke, leaves a person unable to form words.
Trauma, in that scanner, literally deactivated the machinery of speech.

Van der Kolk calls it speechless horror, and it explains something that families and doctors find endlessly frustrating: that people who have been through something terrible often cannot say what happened, not because they are hiding it, and not because they have forgotten, but because in the moment of activation, the part of the brain that makes sentences goes offline.
It also explains, and this is the beginning of the therapeutic argument, why asking someone to talk about it is sometimes a demand they physically cannot meet.

There is a second study that shows how differently this can present, and it involves a Canadian couple, Stan and Ute Lawrence, who were caught in an enormous multi vehicle pile up in dense fog on a major highway.
Both were in the same crash.
Both were traumatised.
But their scans looked like they came from different species.
When Stan was played his script, his brain lit up in the way I have just described: a full blown reliving, panic, the body in emergency.
When Ute was played hers, almost nothing happened.
Her brain went nearly blank.
Activity dropped across the board.
This is dissociation, and van der Kolk's point is that it is not the absence of a trauma response, it is the other trauma response.
Some people go into overdrive.
Others go offline, go numb, vacate the premises.

Both are the nervous system's attempt to survive something unsurvivable, and the second kind is routinely missed, because a person who has shut down looks, from the outside, like a person who is coping.
Now, the nervous system, because this is where the book becomes genuinely practical.
Van der Kolk leans heavily on the work of Stephen Porges, and specifically on the idea that the autonomic nervous system has not two settings but three, arranged in a hierarchy.
The top level is the social engagement system, run through a branch of the vagus nerve.

When you feel safe, this is what is active, and it does something remarkable: it connects the muscles of your face, your voice, your throat, and your middle ear into a single system with your heart and your lungs.
A person in this state has a mobile face, a voice with musical range, relaxed eye contact, and a heart rate that varies gently with the breath.
If safety fails, you drop to the second level: the sympathetic nervous system.
Fight or flight.
Heart rate up, blood to the muscles, face flattens into vigilance.
And if fight or flight fails, or is impossible, you drop to the third and oldest level: the dorsal vagal shutdown.
Collapse, freeze, numbness, the body going limp.
It is the response of an animal in the jaws of a predator, and it is not a choice.
Porges's word for the way the body decides which level to occupy is neuroception, and van der Kolk emphasises that it happens below awareness and faster than thought.
Your nervous system reads the tone of a voice, the tension in a face, the speed of a movement, and it has already responded before you have consciously registered anything.
That framework does an enormous amount of explanatory work.
It tells you why a traumatised person can find an ordinary meeting or a crowded shop physically intolerable, because their neuroception is miscalibrated and reads neutral faces as threats.
It tells you why tone of voice, rhythm, and eye contact are not therapeutic niceties but direct inputs into the regulating system.
And it tells you why the third state, the shutdown, so often gets read as laziness, stubbornness, or lack of motivation, when it is a nervous system in the deepest form of defence available to it.

Which brings van der Kolk to a claim he repeats throughout the book, and which is probably its central practical assertion: being able to feel safe with other people is probably the single most important aspect of mental health.
Safe connections are the foundation of a meaningful life, and the great damage of trauma is that it makes exactly that impossible, by making other human beings feel like the source of the danger.
He builds the case for that starting with infants, and here he uses one of the most famous demonstrations in developmental psychology, Edward Tronick's still face experiment.
A mother sits with her baby, playing, cooing, responding.
Everything is normal.
Then, on instruction, she stops.
She keeps looking at the baby but makes her face completely blank and does not react at all.
The baby tries everything.
Smiles.
Points.
Squeals.
Reaches.
And when none of it produces a response, within about two minutes, the baby becomes distressed, turns away, and begins to collapse into a kind of despair.
What is being demonstrated is that an infant is not simply seeking food and warmth.
It is seeking attunement, the experience of being met, and its whole regulatory system depends on it.

From there van der Kolk goes into attachment research: John Bowlby's original work, Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation experiments, and the long term studies, including a remarkable Minnesota project that followed a group of children from before birth for decades.

The finding that matters here is that the quality of early attunement predicts a striking amount about later life, and that the children who do worst are not necessarily those with the most obviously frightening parents, but those with parents who are simultaneously the source of comfort and the source of fear.
That situation, where the person you must run to for safety is the person you must run from, produces what researchers call disorganised attachment, and it is a form of biological trap.
There is no coherent strategy available.
And van der Kolk argues that it is this, more than any single dramatic event, that produces the deepest and most persistent damage.
Which brings us to the piece of research that, more than anything else in the book, ought to be public knowledge and is not.
In the 1980s, a doctor called Vincent Felitti was running an obesity clinic at Kaiser Permanente in San Diego.
The programme worked.
People lost very large amounts of weight.
And then, at high rates, they dropped out, specifically after succeeding.
People who had lost fifty or a hundred pounds would abandon the programme and regain everything.
Felitti could not understand it, so he started interviewing them.
And in one of those interviews he misspoke.
He meant to ask how old a patient had been when she became sexually active, and instead asked, in effect, how much she weighed at the time.
She answered: forty pounds.
Then she added that she had been four years old, and that it had been with her father.
He began asking others, systematically, and found that a very large proportion of his patients had histories of childhood sexual abuse.
And the weight, which everyone including the patients had understood as a failure of discipline, turned out to be functioning as protection.
Being large kept people at a distance.
Losing weight removed the shield, and the anxiety that followed was worse than the obesity.

Felitti joined with Robert Anda, an epidemiologist at the Centers for Disease Control, and together they ran what became the Adverse Childhood Experiences study, on more than seventeen thousand middle class, mostly employed, mostly insured adults, the least likely population you would expect to find these histories in.

They asked about ten categories of childhood adversity: physical, emotional and sexual abuse, physical and emotional neglect, and household dysfunction including a parent with mental illness, a parent with addiction, an incarcerated household member, domestic violence, and parental separation.
One point per category.
Two thirds of this ordinary, comfortable population reported at least one.
And of those who reported one, the great majority reported more, because these things do not arrive alone.
Then they matched the scores against health outcomes decades later, and the results were not subtle.
The relationship was a clean dose response curve: the higher the score, the worse the outcome, across an enormous range of conditions.

Higher scores tracked with dramatically increased rates of depression, suicide attempts, alcoholism, and injected drug use, with the drug figure at the high end of the scale being a multiple of forty or more compared with a score of zero.
And the outcomes were not only psychiatric.
They included heart disease, liver disease, chronic lung disease, autoimmune conditions, and cancer.
Later analyses of the same data found that people at the top of the range had life expectancies roughly two decades shorter than those at the bottom.
Van der Kolk draws two conclusions from this that are worth sitting with.
The first is that what look like self destructive behaviours are very often solutions.
Smoking, overeating, drinking, drugs, promiscuity, self harm: these are, in the majority of cases, effective short term regulators of an unbearable internal state.
And as Felitti put it, it is extremely hard to give up something that almost works.
Any approach that treats the behaviour as the problem, without addressing what the behaviour is managing, is fighting the wrong war.

The second is that childhood adversity is, in raw public health terms, one of the largest preventable contributors to illness and early death in the developed world, and it is barely treated as a medical issue at all.

Van der Kolk spent years arguing that the diagnostic system needed a category for this, which he proposed as developmental trauma disorder: the specific presentation of a child whose damage came not from a single event but from years of an environment.

Children like this get diagnosed instead with a scattering of separate labels, attention deficit, oppositional defiance, bipolar disorder, conduct disorder, and treated with a corresponding scattering of medications, and van der Kolk is scathing about the resulting rates of antipsychotic prescription in children in state care.
The proposal was rejected by the committee revising the diagnostic manual.
Now, memory, which is the trickiest chapter and the one where he is at his most careful.
The core distinction goes back to the French psychologist Pierre Janet, writing in the 1880s.
Ordinary memory is narrative.
You can tell it, condense it, put it in order, place it in the past, and it changes slightly each time you tell it.
Traumatic memory is not like that.
It arrives whole, in fragments of sensation, unchanged by time: a smell, a sound, a physical sensation, a still image.
It is not filed as something that happened.
It behaves like something that is happening.
Van der Kolk describes running Rorschach inkblot tests on trauma survivors and getting one of two responses.
Some saw the trauma, vividly, in the ink.
Others saw nothing at all, which is almost unheard of in that test and which indicates the same shutdown Ute Lawrence showed in the scanner.

What almost nobody did was use their imagination in the ordinary flexible way, and van der Kolk makes a lot of this: trauma costs people their imagination, the capacity to picture something other than what is, and without that capacity you cannot plan, hope, or play.
On the contested question of whether traumatic memories can be lost and later recovered, he lays out the evidence rather than the rhetoric.

The strongest study he cites followed more than a hundred women who had documented hospital records of sexual abuse in childhood, so the events were established independently of anyone's recollection.
Interviewed as adults, a substantial minority, well over a third, did not report the abuse.
Some of those later recalled it.
The study establishes both that the loss of such memories happens and that later recall happens, while saying nothing whatever about whether any particular recovered memory is accurate.

Van der Kolk is honest about the other side too, and about the era in the 1990s when this became a public controversy: memory is genuinely reconstructive, false memories can be created under suggestive conditions, and confident detailed recall is not proof of accuracy.
He is arguing for holding two uncomfortable things at once, which is not a popular position but is the correct one.
Now the piece that gives the book its title.
Van der Kolk's argument is that because trauma is stored as physical states rather than as stories, it shows up in the body.
People with trauma histories have measurably higher rates of chronic pain, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue, digestive disorders, and autoimmune conditions.
Their stress hormone systems do not switch off properly.
Their immune systems, in some studies, appear to become confused about what is a threat.
And they lose contact with their own internal signals.

He introduces the term alexithymia, which literally means having no words for feelings, and describes patients who genuinely cannot tell you whether they are anxious or angry or hungry, who report their emotional state as a blank or as a physical symptom.
He describes people who cannot recognise themselves in a mirror in any felt sense, and people who have become so effective at not noticing their body that they do not notice serious injury.
He connects this to a specific brain finding.
The regions involved in self sensing, the insula and the midline structures that give you a felt sense of being in a body, show reduced activity in traumatised people.
And the mechanism makes grim sense: if what is happening inside your body is unbearable, then shutting off the channel that reports it is an intelligent adaptation.
It is also the reason people feel dead inside long after they are safe.
From which comes his central therapeutic claim: physical self awareness is the first step in releasing the tyranny of the past.
You cannot process what you cannot feel, and you cannot become present in your life if you have vacated your body.
There is one more concept to put in place before the treatment section, and it is the one van der Kolk considers the true definition of the injury.
Trauma, he argues, is fundamentally about the loss of agency.
Not fear, not memory, not even pain.
Agency: the felt sense that what you do makes a difference to what happens to you.

He draws on a body of animal research, including the classic learned helplessness experiments, in which animals subjected to a stress they can escape behave completely differently from animals subjected to the identical stress with no escape available.
The ones who can act remain functional.
The ones who cannot stop trying, and then stop responding at all, even later, when escape becomes available and is obvious.
The system has learned that action is pointless, and the learning outlasts the conditions that produced it.
That, van der Kolk says, is what a traumatised human being is living inside.
Not simply a bad memory, but a nervous system that has concluded, at a level below language, that nothing it does will change anything.
Which is why the ordinary advice to such a person, to take control of their life, is not merely unhelpful, it is a demand issued in a language their body no longer speaks.
And it explains something he observed again and again in the clinic: that the most powerful moments of recovery were almost never insights.
They were moments of effective action.
Pushing against a therapist's hand and feeling the resistance.
Completing a defensive movement that had been interrupted years earlier.
Standing up on a stage and being heard.
Holding a difficult yoga position and choosing, freely, when to come out of it.
Van der Kolk's phrase for the goal of all this is self leadership: the restoration of the person's ownership of their own body and their own mind.
And he is precise that this is not the same as feeling better.
Plenty of interventions make people feel better temporarily.
The question is whether the person leaves with more agency than they arrived with.
So, treatment.
This is the last third of the book and it is the reason people keep it on the shelf.
Van der Kolk organises the paths to recovery into three, and he is clear that most people need more than one.
The first is top down: talking, understanding, connecting, and making sense of the story.
This is what conventional therapy does, and van der Kolk is emphatic that it is genuinely valuable and genuinely insufficient on its own.
Understanding why you flinch does not stop you flinching.
He puts it memorably: knowing does not equal healing.
A person can have a complete, articulate, accurate account of what happened to them and still have a body that goes into full emergency at a particular tone of voice.
The second is medication.
He is measured here.
Antidepressants help a substantial number of people, sometimes very much.
Sleep medication has its place.

But he is severely critical of the assumption that drugs are the primary intervention, notes that they generally do not resolve the underlying dysregulation, and is at his sharpest on the prescribing of powerful psychiatric drugs to traumatised children.
And the third is bottom up: allowing the body to have experiences that deeply and viscerally contradict the helplessness of the trauma.
This is his real contribution, and everything in the last section is a version of it.
Let me go through the specific approaches he covers.
Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing, or EMDR, developed by Francine Shapiro.
The patient holds the traumatic memory in mind while following the therapist's finger back and forth with their eyes, or receiving some other left to right alternating stimulus.
Van der Kolk was, by his own account, deeply sceptical, thought it looked ridiculous, and then ran a trial and found it worked, sometimes remarkably fast.
He is honest that nobody is sure why.
His own speculation involves its resemblance to the rapid eye movements of dreaming sleep, during which the brain appears to do exactly this kind of integration work.

And he notes something clinically important: EMDR often allows people to process an experience without having to narrate it in detail, which for the speechless horror problem is a very significant advantage.
Yoga.
This began, in van der Kolk's telling, with heart rate variability.
That is a measure of how much your heart rate fluctuates in rhythm with your breathing, and it is a good proxy for how well the calming branch of your nervous system is working.
Traumatised people have poor heart rate variability, which is one reason they are physiologically bad at self soothing.
He looked for interventions that improve it, and the strongest candidate was yoga.
His centre ran a study with women who had severe, long standing post traumatic stress, many of whom had not responded to anything else, using a trauma sensitive yoga programme over about ten weeks.
The improvements were substantial, and van der Kolk notes, pointedly, that the effect compared favourably with the results of medication trials.
But the crucial element is not the postures.
Trauma sensitive yoga is deliberately designed around choice and interoception.
Nobody touches you without asking.
Nobody stands behind you.
Instructors use invitational language rather than commands.

And the actual work is noticing what you feel, holding a position that produces discomfort, discovering that the discomfort has a beginning, a middle and an end, and that you can end it whenever you decide to.
That, in miniature, is the direct experiential contradiction of helplessness.
Neurofeedback.
Sensors read the electrical activity of the brain, and the person is rewarded, usually through a screen or a sound, for producing particular patterns.
Over sessions, the brain learns to hold those patterns.
Van der Kolk devotes a chapter to it, and describes cases, particularly among severely traumatised children and among veterans, where nothing else had worked.
Internal Family Systems, developed by Richard Schwartz, is the approach van der Kolk seems most personally attached to, and it is worth explaining properly because it is unusual.
The model says the mind is naturally made of parts, and that this is not pathology, it is normal architecture.
Everyone has a part that wants to leave the party and a part that wants to stay.
In someone with trauma, these parts become extreme and polarised, and Schwartz sorts them into three types.
There are exiles, the young, wounded parts carrying the pain, the shame and the terror, which the system has locked away because letting them into consciousness is intolerable.
There are managers, the controlling, perfectionist, hypervigilant, people pleasing parts, whose whole job is to run life in a way that ensures the exiles never get triggered.
And there are firefighters, the parts that take emergency action when an exile breaks through anyway: drinking, bingeing, cutting, raging, dissociating, compulsive sex or work.
They are called firefighters because their job is to put out the fire immediately, by any means, without the slightest regard for the damage.

And underneath all of them, the model holds, is the Self, which is not a part but the person's core, and which is characterised by curiosity, calm, compassion and confidence, and which, crucially, is never damaged.
It can be buried, but it cannot be destroyed.
The therapy involves getting to know these parts rather than fighting them, and the founding line of the whole approach is that there are no bad parts.
The firefighter that gets you drunk is not your enemy.
It is a part that has taken on a desperate job, badly, because it was the only job available, and it will stand down when the exile it is protecting is no longer in unbearable pain.
Van der Kolk's clinical point is that this reframing does more to reduce self hatred than almost anything else he has seen, and self hatred is the engine of most of the ongoing damage.

Psychomotor therapy, developed by Albert Pesso, in which a person constructs a physical, three dimensional representation of their history in the room, using other people to stand in for the figures in their life, and then, crucially, is given the experience of what should have happened: an ideal mother who protects, an ideal father who notices.

Van der Kolk's argument is that this creates a new, embodied memory that sits alongside the old one, and that the body responds to it as though it were real, because in terms of the felt sense, it was.
Theatre.
This is the most surprising chapter and the one people are most moved by.

He describes programmes putting traumatised adolescents, including young people in the juvenile justice system, into serious theatre work, including a company in western Massachusetts doing Shakespeare with court involved teenagers, and improvisation programmes in Boston schools.
The reasoning is precise, not sentimental.
Trauma isolates you, and theatre is inescapably collective.
Trauma makes you a passive object, and acting requires agency and voice.
Trauma flattens the body, and stagecraft requires you to inhabit and project physically.
Trauma renders you speechless, and a script hands you enormous words for enormous feelings that are not yours to be ashamed of, because they belong to the character.
A teenager who cannot say a word about his own rage can stand on a stage and be Macbeth.
Writing.

He cites the work of James Pennebaker, whose experiments asked people to write, privately, for around fifteen or twenty minutes on consecutive days about a difficult experience, holding nothing back, with no intention of showing it to anybody.
The people who did so showed measurable improvements in health markers and made fewer visits to the doctor over the following months compared with those who wrote about neutral subjects.
Van der Kolk emphasises the privacy: the point is not communication, it is giving the experience a shape.
He also gives space to the simplest intervention of all, which is other people.
Not therapy, just people.
He describes patients for whom the decisive change was a choir, a congregation, a regular table of friends, a dog, or a job with colleagues who noticed when they did not turn up.
His argument is that the social engagement system is a muscle, that it atrophies in isolation, and that it can only be exercised in the presence of other nervous systems that are themselves calm.
And he is candid about how badly the treatment system is set up for this.
Insurance pays for medication and for a limited number of individual sessions.
It does not pay for a theatre programme, or a martial arts class, or two years of a stable relationship with one clinician, which is frequently what the person actually needs.

Van der Kolk is direct that a great deal of what he considers the most effective work he has seen is unfundable, and that this, rather than any lack of knowledge, is why so many people do not get better.
And running through all of it: rhythm, breath, singing, drumming, dance, martial arts, group movement.

He notes that essentially every culture in human history has responded to collective trauma with rhythm and movement in groups, and that Western psychiatry is close to unique in having decided that the treatment for suffering is a conversation between two people in chairs.
Now let me be a fair guide and tell you where to hold this book loosely.
Van der Kolk is a clinician making a case, and the evidence behind the various therapies he recommends is not uniform in quality.

EMDR has a reasonable evidence base for post traumatic stress, though the specific role of the eye movements remains genuinely disputed and many researchers think the exposure component is doing the work.
The neurofeedback evidence is considerably thinner than the enthusiasm in that chapter suggests.
The polyvagal framework, which does a lot of explanatory work here, is a theory that some researchers regard as underdetermined by the physiological evidence.
And the ACE findings, while robust as correlations, are correlations, in a large retrospective self report study, with all the caveats that implies.

There is also a broader criticism worth knowing: that the popularity of this book has helped push a very expansive idea of trauma into everyday language, so that the word now covers everything from genocide to a difficult week, which risks both trivialising the severe cases and pathologising ordinary distress.
Van der Kolk himself is generally careful, and writes about serious, chronic, life shaping harm, but the culture that grew around the book has not always been.

None of which undermines the central claim, which has held up well and is now fairly mainstream: that trauma is physiological as well as psychological, that it is stored in the body and in automatic response systems rather than only in narrative memory, and that treatments engaging the body and the nervous system directly belong alongside talking rather than after it.
So, practically, what do you do with this?
First, if you recognise yourself in any of it, learn to notice your body on purpose.
Two or three times a day, stop and ask what you actually feel physically: where the tension is, what your breathing is doing, whether your jaw is clenched.
Van der Kolk regards this unglamorous habit as the foundation of everything else, because you cannot regulate a state you cannot detect.
Second, use the breath deliberately, because it is the one part of the autonomic nervous system you have direct manual control over.
Slow exhales, longer out than in, engage the calming branch.
It is not a metaphor.
It is a lever wired into the hardware.
Third, do something rhythmic with other people.
Choir, dance class, team sport, martial arts, drumming, rowing.
Van der Kolk would say that the combination of rhythm, movement, and being in synchrony with other bodies is doing something for the nervous system that no amount of insight can achieve alone.

Fourth, if you are going to try yoga or any body based practice, choose one where the instruction is invitational, where you are never touched without permission, and where you are encouraged to stop at any moment.
The choice is not a courtesy.
The choice is the active ingredient.
Fifth, try Pennebaker's exercise.
Fifteen minutes a day, three or four consecutive days, writing without stopping and without editing about something difficult, and then, if you want to, destroy the pages.
It costs nothing and the evidence behind it is better than most things that cost a great deal.
Sixth, change how you talk to yourself about your worst habits.
Ask what each one is protecting you from, and what would happen if it stopped tomorrow.
That question does more useful work than any amount of resolve, because it addresses the fire rather than the firefighter.

Seventh, if you are close to someone who is struggling, remember the neuroception point: your tone of voice, your face, your pace and your predictability are direct inputs into their nervous system, and they matter more than the content of what you say.
Calm is contagious in the same way panic is.
And eighth, if you are seeking help, look for something that includes the body, and do not accept the idea that understanding your history is the same as being free of it.
I will finish with the man we started with.
Tom, the lawyer who would not take the medication because giving up his nightmares would betray his friends.
What van der Kolk realised, eventually, was that Tom was not being irrational.
He was telling the truth about the structure of his condition.
The symptoms were not merely a malfunction to be switched off.

They were carrying something: loyalty, grief, guilt, and a set of experiences that had never been allowed to become a story, because the part of his brain that makes stories shut down every time he approached them.
That is what the whole book is arguing, in the end.
The body kept the score because the mind was never given the conditions in which it could finish the accounting.

And the work of recovery is not to erase what happened, or to explain it more cleverly, but to give the nervous system enough safety, enough rhythm, enough contradicting experience, and enough company, that it can finally put the event where it belongs.
In the past.
